question: What is the tiny working unit of the kidney that makes urine?
explanation: You've got this! The nephron is the main filtering unit of the kidney that cleans the blood and creates urine. Think of millions of these little guys working hard inside each kidney.

question: Where does the first step of blood filtration happen in the kidney?
explanation: Great try! Blood pressure pushes water and small particles through a tiny ball of capillaries called the glomerulus to start the cleaning process.

question: Which hormone helps your body hold onto water when you are dehydrated?
explanation: Spot on! Antidiuretic hormone (ADH) signals the kidneys to save water and keep you from getting too dried out when fluids are low.

question: What kind of urine do you expect from a patient who is severely dehydrated?
explanation: Makes total sense, right? When the body lacks water, the kidneys hold onto every drop, leaving you with a small amount of dark, concentrated urine.

question: How do the kidneys respond when the blood becomes too acidic?

options.A: By retaining hydrogen ions and excreting bicarbonate
options.B: By secreting hydrogen ions and reabsorbing bicarbonate
options.C: By slowing down the filtration rate of the glomerulus
options.D: By increasing the production of red blood cells

explanation: You're doing great! To balance the pH, the kidneys pump out extra acid (hydrogen ions) in the urine and keep helpful buffers like bicarbonate in the blood.

question: What is the normal healthy pH range for human blood?
explanation: Keep this number in your pocket—a blood pH of 7.35 to 7.45 is a vital sign range that the lungs and kidneys work hard to maintain every single day.

question: Which waste product from muscle breakdown is checked in lab tests to see how well kidneys are working?
explanation: Spot on! Creatinine is a normal waste product from our muscles. If the kidneys aren't filtering well, this level builds up in the blood.

question: What happens to urea and other metabolic waste in a healthy nephron?

options.A: They are converted into useful proteins in the loop of Henle
options.B: They are stored in the renal cortex for later energy use
options.C: They are filtered out of the blood and excreted in urine
options.D: They are reabsorbed entirely to nourish kidney tissue

explanation: Exactly! The body doesn't need these wastes, so the nephrons filter them out of the bloodstream so they can leave the body in urine.

question: What enzyme do the kidneys release when blood pressure drops too low?
explanation: You've got this! Specialized cells in the kidney release renin to start a chain reaction that brings blood pressure back up where it belongs.

question: What is the main job of angiotensin II in the body?

options.A: Stopping all fluid movement through the capillary walls
options.B: Dilating peripheral blood vessels to lower heart rate
options.C: Constricting blood vessels to raise blood pressure
options.D: Increasing the heart's pumping speed without changing vessel size

explanation: Think of angiotensin II as a quick-fix squeeze: it tightens up your blood vessels so your blood pressure goes right back up when circulation drops.

question: Which hormone do the kidneys produce to tell the bone marrow to make red blood cells?
explanation: Brilliant! When oxygen levels drop, the kidneys send out erythropoietin (EPO) as a rescue signal to the bone marrow to make more red blood cells.

question: Why do patients with long-term kidney disease often suffer from severe anemia?

options.A: Damaged kidneys fail to produce enough erythropoietin
options.B: Uremic toxins coat the lungs and prevent oxygen uptake
options.C: The renal tubules destroy mature red blood cells directly
options.D: High blood pressure causes red blood cells to burst

explanation: Makes complete sense! If the kidneys are damaged, they can't make enough EPO, so the bone marrow doesn't get the signal to pump out fresh red blood cells.

question: What is the final active form of vitamin D made by the kidneys?
explanation: You're doing great! The kidneys put the finishing touch on vitamin D by turning it into calcitriol, which keeps your bones strong and healthy.

question: What is the main job of active vitamin D once processed by the kidneys?

options.A: To lower blood pressure by widening blood vessels
options.B: To speed up the filtration rate of the glomerulus
options.C: To stimulate red blood cell production in marrow
options.D: To promote calcium and phosphorus absorption in the gut

explanation: Spot on! Active vitamin D helps your intestines absorb calcium and phosphorus from your food so your body has what it needs for strong bones.

question: What process do the kidneys use to make new sugar during long periods of fasting?
explanation: You've got this! When you haven't eaten in a while and need energy, your kidneys can actually build new glucose (gluconeogenesis) to keep your blood sugar stable.

question: When are your kidneys most likely to start producing extra glucose?

options.C: A sudden spike in blood pressure

explanation: Exactly right! When liver energy stores run out during a long fast, the kidneys step up and make glucose to help keep your body fueled.
